easy.heading: Warming Up With The Basics
easy.body:
I started my morning with the easy grid, and it was such a pleasant way to wake up my brain. The first thing that caught my eye was that sum of 11 in the top left corner. Since the highest number on a domino is 6, I knew I had to use a 5 and a 6 or maybe two 5s if they were part of different dominoes. I placed the [5,5] domino vertically at (1,0) and (0,0), which made (0,0) a five. That meant (0,1) had to be a six to reach that 11 total.

From there, everything just clicked. The [3,6] domino fit perfectly into cells (0,1) and (0,2), which gave me a three at (0,2). I then looked at the sum of 9 region involving (0,2), (1,1), and (1,2). With the three already there, I just needed the other two cells to add up to six. By using the [3,0] and [2,3] dominoes in the remaining spots, I was able to satisfy those equals constraints at the bottom and finish the whole grid in no time.

medium.heading: Stepping It Up A Notch
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today had a few more twists, especially with that big sum of 12 at the bottom. Since I did not have a double-six domino, I had to figure out which two dominoes could provide sixes for cells (3,1) and (3,2). I ended up using the [6,4] and [2,6] dominoes, which really helped narrow down the possibilities for the rest of the bottom row. I placed the [6,4] domino horizontally across (3,1) and (3,0), putting the 6 in the sum region.

The middle of the grid was where I spent the most time. There were several small sum regions, like the sum of 4 at (2,1) and (2,2) and the sum of 6 at (2,3) and (3,3). I had to be careful not to use up my low-value dominoes too quickly. The [2,2] domino was a lifesaver for the sum of 4 region. Once those were in place, the [3,4] and [6,0] dominoes found their homes in the remaining sections quite naturally. It was a nice challenge that required looking a few steps ahead.

hard.heading: A Real Brain Buster For Saturday
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today really made me work for it! The grid was much larger, and those long equals constraints were everywhere. I started by looking for the easiest wins, which were the sum of 0 regions. Since only a blank side of a domino can make a zero, I knew those cells had to be pips-free. I focused on (0,3), (0,4), (2,1), (4,4), and (5,4) as they were all part of sum 0 regions. This immediately told me that dominoes like [0,0], [1,0], and [4,0] were going to be used as anchors.

The real breakthrough came when I looked at the long equals regions. There was a section where four different cells had to have the same value. I had to balance the [5,3] and [6,3] dominoes very carefully to make sure the math worked out for both the sums and the equals signs. There was a moment where I thought I had messed up because I had a [1,1] left over, but I realized it fit perfectly in the middle after I shifted the [5,2] domino. It felt so satisfying when that final piece, the [4,4], slid into its spot at the end.

explanation.tips: Always look for the most restrictive rules first, like a sum of 0 or a very high sum target. These usually only have one or two possible domino combinations. Also, use the equals signs to your advantage by tracking values across the grid, as they often link several dominoes together and force their orientation.
explanation.learned:
I learned today that empty cells are not just dead space; they are actually helpful boundaries that limit which way a domino can face. If you see an empty marker, use it to rule out any dominoes that would need to cross over that cell.

I also realized that in the larger puzzles, the less than constraints are amazing for ruling out your heavy-hitter dominoes early on. Saving those high-value pieces like the [5,5] or [6,3] for the specific sum targets makes the whole process much smoother.

faqs.question: How do you find the starting point in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: Look for the smallest or largest sum targets first. A sum of 0 or a sum of 12 has very few domino combinations, which makes them the perfect place to start.

faqs.question: What does a sum of 0 mean in a Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: A sum of 0 means every cell in that highlighted region must contain zero pips. You will need to use dominoes that have a blank side to fill these spots.

faqs.question: Are there always enough dominoes to fill the grid?
faqs.answer: Yes, the list of dominoes provided is exactly what you need to fill every cell. Each domino is used exactly once.

faqs.question: How do the equals symbols work in the grid?
faqs.answer: The equals symbol between cells means those specific cells must have the exact same number of pips, even if they are part of different dominoes or different regions.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for Hard Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: Focus on the long regions that span across multiple dominoes. These often create a chain reaction where one placement forces the next three or four pieces into place.

faqs.question: Can I use the same domino twice in one day?
faqs.answer: No, each puzzle uses a specific set of unique dominoes. Once you use the [5,5] in a grid, you cannot use it again in that same puzzle.
